criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to urban basic services, explicitly focusing on water, sanitation, and electricity in poor urban townships, informal settlements, and inner-city buildings in South Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the chapter examines constitutional/statutory frameworks, municipal governance failures, protests, and socio-economic rights litigation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it also examines concrete legal and administrative rules directly governing service access, including Free Basic Water (FBW) volume/tariff rules (6 kilolitres per household per month), pre-paid water meter (PPM) automatic disconnection mechanisms and municipal bylaws, pre-disconnection notice and procedural fairness rules under PAJA and Section 4(3) of the Water Services Act, municipal requirements for a landlord letter of permission before contracting with inner-city tenants, and informal settlement upgrading rules under the National Housing Code (Mazibuko, Joseph, and Nokotyana). However, the chapter is excluded under Criterion 3 (E05) on both readings.
criterion_notes.c3: Book chapter providing a preliminary legal, policy, and socio-political narrative overview rather than an empirical study or systematic empirical synthesis. Sections 2-5 synthesize constitutional/statutory doctrine, previously published reports (e.g. Tissington et al. 2008; Jain 2010; Sinwell et al. 2009), and media coverage; Section 6 applies a conceptual typology to summarize three Constitutional Court test cases (Joseph, Mazibuko, Nokotyana) using court judgments, secondary literature (including Dugard 2009, 2010), and brief anecdotal/email updates, with no empirical study design or systematic data collection methodology.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses outcomes directly relevant to water and sanitation access, including disconnections for non-payment, pre-paid meter cutoffs, water sufficiency (litres per person per day), affordability, communal tap and sanitation availability in informal settlements, and post-litigation policy adjustments.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the chapter is a non-empirical narrative overview spanning national legislation, secondary protest reports, and three distinct Constitutional Court lawsuits without primary empirical methods or systematic review procedures, an empirical study design and study sample are not identifiable.

raw_response.exposure: South African constitutional and statutory basic-service framework, municipal credit-control and service-delivery rules (Free Basic Water 6 kl limit, pre-paid water meters, pre-disconnection notice requirements under PAJA and municipal bylaws, landlord permission requirements, informal settlement upgrading rules), local protests, and test-case litigation
raw_response.outcome: Household and community access to water, sanitation, and electricity services, including disconnections, water quantity/sufficiency, affordability, communal tap/toilet provision, and post-litigation policy and bylaw changes
raw_response.population_and_sample: Poor urban residents in South Africa (townships, informal settlements, and inner-city buildings) discussed across secondary studies, protest reports, and three Constitutional Court cases (Joseph, Mazibuko, Nokotyana); no primary empirical sample
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (no empirical evidence). Although this book chapter examines household water and sanitation access in urban South Africa (c1=yes) and discusses concrete legal and administrative rule-type mechanisms governing access—such as Free Basic Water allocations, pre-paid water meter rules, PAJA/statutory pre-disconnection notice rules, and landlord permission rules for tenant utility contracts (c2=yes under both plain and narrow readings)—it is a narrative legal/policy and socio-political overview chapter rather than an empirical study or systematic empirical synthesis. It synthesizes statutes, secondary reports, media accounts of service-delivery protests, and three Constitutional Court judgments (Joseph, Mazibuko, Nokotyana) within a conceptual typology of litigation impact, without an identifiable empirical study design, sampling frame, or systematic primary data collection/analysis method (c3=no, c5=no).
raw_response.study_design: Non-empirical legal, policy, and socio-political narrative overview chapter
